card st-build-card  [decided]
Every build opens a card obligation, and the pass closes it with a card or with the cards it followed
why: The obligation is data in the log, so a pass that changes code and leaves the map untouched shows as an open obligation. A pass that made no new decision closes it by naming the cards its choices came from, so it never writes a card only to meet a quota.

The CLI command that starts a build appends the obligation to the log, before any code is written.

When the pass writes a card, the agent places it: the title, the why, the parent in the refines tree, the depends_on. The CLI cannot choose the parent, because knowing what a decision refines is judgment. So the pipeline creates the demand and the agent satisfies it.

Nothing here can drift, because the obligation is data in the log rather than a line in a prompt. An unsatisfied one is visible in the map.

A pass closes the obligation in one of two ways. It proposes one card for each decision that no card gives: a pass that makes three decisions writes three. Or, when every choice in its diff came from a cited card or from a card its search found, it records "no new decision" and names those cards. The grader checks that record against the diff the same way it checks the cited cards. A choice in the diff that none of the named cards gives fails the pass as an unrecorded decision. A list of values, a configuration, or the inside of one helper is not a decision, so it is never a reason to write a card.

Example:

- Card A "Each agent carries its role outside the prompt".
- Ticket T "Show the role in the launch record", which cites A.
- Pass P builds T.

1. The build starts. The log gets obligation O for P, and the map shows O open.
2. P adds the role to the launch record. Every choice comes from A. P records "no new decision" and names A. O closes.
3. The grader reads the diff. Each choice traces to A, so the pass goes on.
4. P also picks a new file format that A does not give, and names only A. The grader fails the pass as an unrecorded decision. The next pass proposes a card for the format, and that card closes O.
5. P exits with neither a card nor a record. O stays open on the map.

```
build starts ──> obligation O (open)
                      │
pass P ──┬── a decision no card gives ──> proposes card C ──> O closed by C
         └── every choice from cards ──> "no new decision: A" ──> O closed
                                               │
                       grader: a choice in the diff that A does not give ──> pass fails

O = the card obligation of one build   A = a card the pass names   C = a card the pass proposes
```

Building the "no new decision" part of `#st-build-card` needs one more decision: the form of the command that writes that record.

**What the card asks for.** A pass closes its card obligation in one of two ways:

1. It proposes a card. This works today: `werk add ... --obligation <id>` closes the obligation.
2. It records "no new decision" and names the cards it followed. Nothing can write this today. The builder agent has no verb or flag that says "obligation O is closed, the choices came from cards A and B". `werk-v0` has none either.

**Why that blocks the code.** The map rules keep every command's verb, flags and output on one card under `#werk-cli`. No such card exists for this record yet. So the build would have to make up the form, and that is a decision no card gives.

**The fix is small.** It is a "me" decision because it is easy to reverse. There are two readings:

1. A new verb: `werk followed <obligation> --cards a,b`.
2. A flag on an existing verb, for example `werk status`, or a new `werk obligation close`.

I recommend reading 1, because the record is its own event in the log. I can propose the command card under `#werk-cli` now. After you accept it, `#st-build-card` moves from "blocked" to "next".

card werk-cli-add  [decided]
`werk add` proposes a card, an option or a source as a ghost
why: Every new node enters the map through one command, so the ghost rule holds for every kind.

```
werk add <id> --title "..." [--why "..."] [--body "..."] [--parent <id>]
         [--kind card|option|source] [--status open|proto] [--who you|me|prototype]
         [--why_not "..."]              for --kind option
         [--url ...] [--finding ...]    for --kind source
```

- The command prints "proposed". No flag skips the ghost (#werk-propose-new).
- `--status decided` is refused. A card reaches decided only through `werk status` (#werk-contract-when).
- A second `werk add` with the same id fails. `werk edit --body`, `werk edit --why` and `werk retitle` refuse on a ghost. `werk link`, `werk status` and `werk edit --who` work on a ghost.
- A rejected option takes two commands: `werk add <id>:opt0 --kind option --title "..." --why_not "..."`, then `werk link <id>:opt0 <id> --type alternative_to` (#ro-live, #ro-optparent).

  -> refines         werk-cli  The CLI is the agent's interface to the map. Each command's form lives on one card under it
  -> depends_on      werk-propose-new  A new card is a proposal too, not a direct append
       why: The command stages every kind as a ghost and refuses a word change on one, as this card requires.
  -> depends_on      werk-contract-when  The check fires at the move to decided, not at creation
       why: The refusal of --status decided comes from the rule that decided is reached only through the decide check.
  -> depends_on      ro-live  Record a rejected option the moment it's weighed, not after
       why: The option form of the command records the rejected alternative that this card requires.
  -> depends_on      ro-optparent  An option links to its card by alternative_to only, never by refines
       why: The option recipe links by alternative_to only, because this card forbids a refines link from an option.
  <- alternative_to  werk-cli-add:opt0  `werk add` refuses a card with no `--status`
Options
  werk-cli-add:opt0  `werk add` refuses a card with no `--status`
    why not: A new card is nearly always open, so the agent would type the same flag every time. A refusal costs a failed call for no gain, and open is the safe default.

card st-build-card  [decided]
Every build opens a card obligation, and the pass closes it with a card or with the cards it followed

I proposed `#werk-cli-followed` under `#werk-cli` as a ghost. It waits for your ✓.

- **Form:** `werk followed <obligation-id> --cards a,b`. It appends one event to the log, closes the obligation, and prints the cards it followed.
- **Refusals (exit 1, nothing written):** a named card that is not decided, an unknown obligation, an obligation that is already closed, or no `--cards`.
- **Accept:** none needed. The record is a fact in the log, and the grader checks it against the diff.
- **Links:** `depends_on #st-build-card`. That target is decided and not stale.
- **Rejected option:** `:opt0` "A flag on an existing verb closes the obligation".

After you accept it, `#st-build-card` moves from "blocked" to "next" in the plan.

- **Builder prompt:** it offers two ways to close the obligation. A is a card for each new decision. B is `werk followed <obligation> --cards a,b`, and it says the grader checks that record. The "owes at least one card" quota text is gone.
- **Grader:** when a pass recorded "no new decision", the grader prompt gets a fourth line, `unrecorded-decision`. It also gets the full text of the named cards.
  - A choice in the diff that none of those cards gives scores low. That fails the pass.
  - The next pass's brief says "an unrecorded decision (propose a card for it)".
  - A build with no record gets no extra line.
- **Map:** an open obligation shows as a grey alarm on the root and on each card its ticket cites. It disappears when a card or a record closes it. Open `#st-build-card` in `node src/cli.ts serve` to see the alarm.

**Tests:**
- Four new grader prompt tests and two new brief tests.
- Two new build tests. In the first, pass 1 records "no new decision" and the grader scores the unrecorded line 2, so pass 2 gets that gap in its brief and goes green. In the second, a build with no record gets no extra line.
- Full suite on the last run: 976 passed, 2 failed.
- The two failures are overseer and headless timing tests (the silence windows are 300–400 ms). A different one failed on each earlier run, and the rest passed alone or on a rerun, so they are flaky under load. I did not touch that code.
